title: Photosynthesis: full practice quiz
instructions: 18 questions on the week 5 handout. Answer, check, and read each explanation before moving on. At the end, tap **Copy results for Claude** and paste them back into the chat.

questions.explanation: The handout names plants, algae and cyanobacteria as the organisms that turn light energy into chemical energy.

questions.prompt: Organisms that make their own food from inorganic molecules are called ________.
questions.explanation: Autotrophs, also called producers, make their own food, which is why almost every food chain starts with them.

questions.prompt: What are the products of the overall photosynthesis reaction?
questions.explanation: $6\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 6\,\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} + 6\,\mathrm{O_2}$: carbon dioxide and water go in, glucose and oxygen come out.

questions.prompt: Carbon dioxide enters the leaf through the xylem.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide enters through the **stomata**. The xylem brings water from the roots.

options: Chlorophyll reflects green light and absorbs mainly red and blue
questions.hint: We see the colors a pigment does *not* absorb.
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green, so green light reaches our eyes.
Thylakoids are stacked into piles called grana (one stack is a granum).

questions.prompt: In the light-dependent reactions, what is the energy released by electrons moving along the electron transport chain used for?
options: Pumping protons (H⁺) into the thylakoid space
questions.explanation: The energy pumps protons into the thylakoid space, building the gradient that ATP synthase uses.

questions.prompt: The oxygen released by photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: It comes from **water**, split during photolysis. Experiments labelling water with a heavy oxygen isotope found the label in the released O₂.

questions.prompt: At the end of the electron transport chain, electrons reduce NADP⁺ to ________.
questions.explanation: NADPH carries those electrons to the Calvin cycle.

questions.prompt: Describe how light energy ends up stored in ATP and NADPH.
questions.modelAnswer: Light excites electrons in chlorophyll in the photosystems. The electrons pass along an electron transport chain, and the energy released pumps protons into the thylakoid space. Protons flowing back out through ATP synthase drive the making of ATP. At the end of the chain the electrons reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH.
keyPoints: Electron transport chain pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid space
H⁺ flowing back through ATP synthase makes ATP
Electrons finally reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH
questions.explanation: Protons, not electrons, flow through ATP synthase. That's the most common slip on this question.

questions.prompt: In the reduction phase of the Calvin cycle, what does NADPH do?
questions.hint: ATP and NADPH have different jobs here.
questions.explanation: NADPH supplies the electrons and ATP supplies the energy to turn 3-PGA into G3P.

questions.prompt: Carbon fixation produces an unstable six-carbon molecule that splits into two three-carbon molecules of ________.
questions.explanation: Rubisco attaches CO₂ to RuBP; the six-carbon product splits into two 3-PGA.

questions.prompt: How many turns of the Calvin cycle are needed to make one glucose molecule?
questions.hint: One G3P leaves for every 3 CO₂ fixed, and glucose needs 2 G3P.
questions.explanation: Each turn fixes one CO₂. One G3P leaves per 3 CO₂, glucose needs 2 G3P, so 6 CO₂: six turns.

questions.prompt: Most of the G3P made in the Calvin cycle is used to regenerate RuBP.
questions.explanation: Most G3P (with more ATP) rebuilds RuBP; only one G3P per three CO₂ leaves the cycle.

questions.prompt: Explain the significance of the enzyme **Rubisco**.
questions.modelAnswer: Rubisco carries out carbon fixation, attaching CO₂ to RuBP. This is the step where carbon from the air enters the Calvin cycle and ends up in G3P, from which plants build glucose, sucrose, starch and other organic molecules. Because it's an enzyme, it's also why temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis.
keyPoints: Entry point of CO₂ into the Calvin cycle
Leads to G3P and the plant's organic molecules
As an enzyme, links temperature to the rate
questions.explanation: "Explain the significance" wants the role *and* why it matters more widely.

questions.prompt: A plant is in bright light at a warm temperature, but the CO₂ concentration is very low. What happens if the light gets even brighter?
options: The rate stays about the same, because CO₂ is limiting
The rate falls because enzymes denature
questions.explanation: The factor in shortest supply (here CO₂) limits the rate; raising the others won't help until it's increased.

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis falls at high temperatures.
questions.modelAnswer: The Calvin cycle depends on enzymes such as Rubisco. Up to an optimum, higher temperature speeds the reactions up, but beyond the optimum the enzymes start to denature, so the rate falls.
keyPoints: The Calvin cycle relies on enzymes such as Rubisco
Rate rises up to an optimum temperature
Above the optimum, enzymes denature, so the rate falls

questions.prompt: Compare the light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle by location, inputs and outputs, and explain why the Calvin cycle stops in the dark.
questions.modelAnswer: Light-dependent reactions: in the thylakoid membranes; use light and water (and NADP⁺); produce ATP, NADPH and O₂. Calvin cycle: in the stroma; uses CO₂, ATP and NADPH; produces G3P. The Calvin cycle doesn't use light directly, but in the dark the light-dependent reactions stop making ATP and NADPH, so it soon runs out and stops.
keyPoints: Inputs: light and water vs CO₂, ATP and NADPH
Outputs: ATP, NADPH and O₂ vs G3P
Dark: no new ATP and NADPH, so the Calvin cycle stops
questions.explanation: Your lecturer flagged this comparison as an exam essential.
